title: Simone Weil
keyWorks: “The Iliad, or the Poem of Force” (1940)
“Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies” (1942)
summary: Simone Weil was a French philosopher, teacher and mystic who worked in a factory to understand the lives of workers and stood all her life on the side of those who struggle. Her central idea is attention: the ability to see reality and another person clearly, without the distortions of imagination. She wrote about the “gravity” of the soul and about “grace,” about the need for roots, and about how affliction wounds a person.
onEmotions: Weil described the life of the soul through the image of “gravity”: feelings pull us downward on their own, like a law of nature, and willpower alone is not enough. The opposite of gravity is “grace” — what comes as a gift. Imagination, in Weil's view, hurries to fill every void with comforting or frightening pictures; attention — patient, open, unstrained — brings us back to reality. She described “malheur” (affliction) — a fusion of pain and humiliation that leaves shame in the soul, as if the person were to blame. Her notion of “decreation” is not self-destruction (Weil herself distinguished the two) but loosening the ego's grip to make room for the world and for others.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is understandable: the mind runs into the future and paints threats there. Simone Weil wrote a great deal about imagination as a force that “fills the void”: when we don't know what will happen, imagination hurries to complete the picture — often in the darkest colors. She saw “attention” as its opposite: the ability to stop and look at what is, without rushing to interpret it. Attention, for Weil, is not a strained effort but rather an open, patient waiting. From this point of view, anxiety is imagination with nothing to lean on. You don't need to drive it away by force. You can gently bring your attention back to the present moment — to what is actually in front of you, not what fear has sketched in.
anxiety.practice: Choose one object near you and look at it for a whole minute, noticing its details. If your thoughts run off into the future, gently bring them back to the object.

fear.text: Fear is a natural response, and Simone Weil took it seriously. In The Need for Roots she drew up a list of the “needs of the soul” — things a person cannot fully live without, just as with food and sleep. One of them is security: a state in which the soul is not constantly weighed down by fear or terror. Weil believed that constant fear wounds the soul rather than hardening it. Yet she also named risk as a need — a meaningful encounter with danger that awakens courage. From this point of view, your fear is a signal of a real need, not a weakness. You might ask: what kind of security am I missing right now — and where could I find at least a little of it?
fear.practice: Finish the sentence: “I would feel calmer if…” Notice whether there is anything in it you could do today.

sadness.text: Sadness pulls you down, and that is not your fault. Simone Weil described the life of the soul through the image of physical gravity: feelings, in her view, naturally sink downward, like a falling stone. This is not a reproach but an observation: this is how human nature works. The opposite of gravity she called “grace” — what comes not from our effort but as a gift, sometimes unexpectedly. For Weil, a believer, this was connected with God, but a reader without faith can understand her thought too: not everything that lifts us is something we can produce ourselves. From this point of view, sadness doesn't need to be overcome by a lunge of will. You can acknowledge its weight and remain open to what may come on its own.
sadness.practice: Let yourself sit with the sadness for a few minutes without trying to fix it. Notice where in your body you feel this heaviness.

quote.text: All the natural movements of the soul are controlled by laws analogous to those of physical gravity. Grace is the only exception.
quote.author: Simone Weil

grief.text: Grief is an enormous pain, and there is no need to hurry it. Simone Weil wrote about how hard it is to accept a void: the soul strives with all its might to fill it with something — imagined conversations, reproaches, fantasies of how things might have gone differently. Weil called such fillers “compensations.” She did not demand that we give them up through effort; she spoke of the courage to leave the place empty, at least for a while. From her point of view, one could say that grief is love from which presence has been taken away. Love for someone absent, Weil believed, can be very pure: it no longer expects anything in return. Longing does not make your love smaller, and absence does not cancel what was.
grief.practice: Give one minute of silence to the person you have lost — saying nothing and asking nothing of yourself. Simply stay with it.

loneliness.text: Loneliness is hard, especially when it seems that no one sees what is happening to you. For Simone Weil, attention to another person was the highest form of love. She wrote that true love of one's neighbor begins with a simple but very rare ability — to genuinely ask another person what they are going through, and to listen to the answer. From this point of view, one could say that loneliness is a hunger for that kind of attention. It is legitimate and does not make you weak. At the same time, Weil valued solitude: in silence, attention can grow deeper. Perhaps the first step is to give that attention to yourself, and the second is to look for people capable of it — or to give it to someone else.
loneliness.practice: Ask yourself the way you would ask someone close to you: “What are you going through right now?” — and write down an honest answer.

anger.text: Anger is often born from an encounter with injustice, and Simone Weil knew this firsthand: she worked in factories, went to the Spanish war, and all her life took the side of the oppressed. In her essay “The Iliad, or the Poem of Force” she showed how violence turns a person into a thing — both the one it is aimed at and the one who wields it. She noticed that people tend to pass the pain done to them on to others. From her point of view, one could say that anger is legitimate, but its weight easily “spills over” onto others. Weil suggested keeping your attention on the injustice itself — seeing it clearly, without turning away — and not letting pain turn us into transmitters of force.
anger.practice: Feel the anger in your body without letting it out: where is it, what is it like? Then name in one sentence what injustice it has seen.

shame.text: Shame can burn very fiercely, and Simone Weil understood where it often comes from. She described a particular state — “malheur,” usually translated as “affliction”: a fusion of pain, humiliation and social rejection. Weil noticed with remarkable precision that such affliction leaves a brand of shame and self-contempt on the soul, as though the person were to blame for what happened to them. Importantly, she described this as a consequence of pain, not as the truth about the person. From this point of view, one could say that shame is sometimes not the voice of conscience but the trace of a wound. It speaks of what happened to you, not of who you are. You can look at such shame with compassion rather than agreeing with it.
shame.practice: Ask yourself: is this shame about something I did, or about something that was done to me? Write down the answer without judging it.

guilt.text: Guilt shows that other people matter to you. Simone Weil opened The Need for Roots with the idea that the notion of obligation comes before the notion of rights: first and foremost, we owe something to one another. From this point of view, guilt is a living sense of obligation. But Weil also noticed a trap: attention can quietly turn toward oneself — toward one's own image, toward the question “how bad am I?” Then guilt becomes a circle with “I” at its center once again. From her point of view, one could say that the way out is to bring your attention back to the person you feel guilty toward: what do they need now? In this way guilt turns from self-flagellation into care, and care can be expressed in a concrete act.
guilt.practice: Shift your attention from yourself to the other person: what does the person you feel guilty toward need right now? Write down one answer.

envy.text: Everyone knows envy, and Simone Weil did not consider herself above it. She wrote that the soul, feeling an inner emptiness, reaches for whatever might fill it — this is part of what she called “gravity.” From her point of view, one could say that envy is a gaze fixed on the imagined fullness of someone else's life. We see in another what we lack and fill in the rest. Weil set attention to reality against imagination — including attention to your own life, just as it is. There is no need to be ashamed of envy; it shows what you want. But you can gently turn it around: not “why do they have that?” but “what in my own life have I not looked at attentively for a long time?”
envy.practice: Write down exactly what stirs your envy. Then name one thing in your own life that you haven't looked at attentively for a long time.

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy can be very heavy, and they are neither laziness nor weakness. In Simone Weil's writing the word “void” has an unusual meaning. She believed that the soul fears the void and hurries to fill it with anything at all — distractions, imagination, busyness. But in her view, it is precisely the void that can become the place where something new and real one day enters — what she called “grace.” This doesn't mean emptiness is pleasant or that you should seek it out. It means it is not necessarily final. From Weil's point of view, you need not fight emptiness with all your strength; you can let it be, like an empty place at the table where a guest may still arrive.
emptiness.practice: Sit for two minutes doing nothing and filling the time with nothing. Simply notice what happens — without demanding that you feel anything.

quote.text: Grace fills empty spaces, but it can only enter where there is a void to receive it.
quote.author: Simone Weil

confusion.text: Confusion is unpleasant: you want to find an answer right away. In her essay on school studies, Simone Weil described attention in a special way. In her view, attention is not tension or a furrowed brow but the ability to suspend thought, leaving it free and open, ready to receive whatever comes. She compared it to solving a difficult geometry problem: the answer often appears not through pressure but through patient waiting. From her point of view, one could say that confusion is not a failure but a moment when the ready-made answers have run out. Instead of grabbing the first solution that turns up, you can stay with the question. Such waiting is not passivity but a special form of attention.
confusion.practice: Write down your main question in one sentence. Don't answer it — just reread it slowly a few times and see what changes.

fatigue.text: Tiredness and burnout are real, and Simone Weil knew them from the inside. A philosophy teacher, she went to work in a factory for a year to understand the lives of workers, and she described how exhausting, monotonous labor under time pressure crushes the very ability to think. She did not see this as a personal weakness of the workers: the problem lay in the conditions. From her point of view, one could say that burnout is not your personal failure but the result of being asked, for a long time, for more than a human being can bear. Weil also noticed that we often confuse attention with muscular strain. Real attention doesn't require clenched teeth. Perhaps what matters now is not to strain harder but to loosen your grip.
fatigue.practice: Notice where in your body you are “holding” tension right now — your jaw, shoulders, forehead. Let that place go for a few exhalations.

boredom.text: Boredom can be agonizing. Simone Weil has an unexpected thought: what is truly boring is not the good but the imaginary. Daydreams, fantasies, invented dramas seem vivid but quickly repeat themselves; reality, if you look at it attentively, is always new. From this point of view, one could say that boredom is not a sign that the world is poor but a sign that attention is tired of gliding over the surface. Weil taught an “attentive gaze”: looking at a thing, a person or a task so long and so openly that it begins to reveal itself. Boredom then is an invitation not to new entertainments but to a slower, deeper look at what is already near you.
boredom.practice: Choose something very ordinary — a cup, a leaf, your own hand — and describe it with ten details you hadn't noticed before.

quote.text: Imaginary evil is romantic and varied; real evil is gloomy, monotonous, barren, boring. Imaginary good is boring; real good is always new, marvellous, intoxicating.
quote.author: Simone Weil

joy.text: Joy is precious, and Simone Weil, for all the rigor of her thought, took it very seriously. She wrote that joy and pain are equally precious gifts, and each deserves to be lived fully, in its purity, without mixing one with the other. For Weil, joy is connected with the beauty of the world and with a sense of reality: in joy we feel especially clearly that the world exists. From this point of view, your joy needs neither justifying nor “diluting” with worries that it will pass. You can simply be in it wholly, with attention. Attentive joy, for Weil, is no less deep than suffering — and no less true.
joy.practice: Pause for a minute and live this joy fully: notice how it feels in your body, what you see and hear right now.

love.text: For Simone Weil, love and tenderness are inseparable from attention. To love, for her, means to see the other as they are, not as our imagination or our desires paint them. She wrote that love needs reality. Real attention means setting yourself aside for a while to make room for the other. This is not erasing yourself but generosity. From this point of view, your tenderness is not just a pleasant feeling but a particular way of looking: carefully, patiently, with interest in who this person really is. Such attention, for Weil, is a rare gift, and it can be given in the simplest things: in the way you listen.
love.practice: In your next conversation with someone close, listen to them without planning your reply. Simply follow what they are saying.

quote.text: Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.
quote.author: Simone Weil

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm and deep feeling. Simone Weil wrote a great deal about the beauty of the world as something given to us without any merit of our own. The sun shines on everyone, the rain falls for everyone; the world, in her view, is full of gifts we did not earn. For Weil, a believer, this was grace, but a non-religious reader can understand her thought too: much of what is good in life comes not as a reward but as a gift. From this point of view, gratitude is attention to the gift. It arises when we notice what we usually take for granted. This is exactly what Weil taught — to see what is, clearly and openly — and gratitude becomes the natural response to such a gaze.
gratitude.practice: Name three things that came to you today without any effort on your part — even the simplest ones.

hope.text: Hope is an important feeling, and Simone Weil had a special word for it: waiting. One of her books is called Waiting for God. For Weil, waiting is neither passive inaction nor an attempt to seize the future, but patient openness. She wrote that we receive the most precious things not when we chase them but when we know how to wait for them. From this point of view, one could say that hope is not a demand made of the future but an attentive readiness for what it may bring. Such hope doesn't break under delays, because it isn't tied to deadlines. It simply stays open. You can cherish your hope without clenching it in your fist.
hope.practice: Think about what you hope for and tell yourself: “I am waiting for this openly, without demanding it.” Notice whether anything shifts inside.

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a longing for the past, and Simone Weil understood its value. In The Need for Roots she wrote that the past is one of the most vital needs of the human soul. We are nourished by what we have received from the past: from family, place, language, traditions. Weil wrote with alarm about how easily the past is destroyed and how hard it is to bring back. From this point of view, nostalgia is neither a weakness nor an escape from the present but a sign that the soul is looking for its roots. This doesn't mean you should live in the past. It means the past can be carefully kept as a source of nourishment — remembered not only with sadness but also with gratitude for what was.
nostalgia.practice: Recall one detail from the past that still nourishes you. How could you keep it in your life today — through an object, an activity, a word?

craving.text: A sharp craving can be very strong, and there is nothing shameful in it. Simone Weil wrote about “gravity” — the soul's natural drive to fill a void with something that brings quick relief. She did not condemn this drive; she saw it as part of human nature. Weil also spoke of the soul's hunger: the danger is not that we are hungry but that we can mistake one thing for another. From her point of view, one could say that a craving often points to a real need — for calm, closeness, rest, meaning — which something is trying to replace. A craving comes in a wave: it rises and falls. You might try not to fight it but to look at it attentively: what hunger is hidden beneath it?
craving.practice: When the craving rises, ask yourself: “What am I really missing right now?” Write down the first answer that comes.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure and not proof of weak character. Simone Weil described the life of the soul through the image of gravity: habits and desires pull us down almost like a law of nature, and willpower alone is often not enough to resist them. She generally did not trust “clenched teeth.” Change, for Weil, comes through attention and through what doesn't depend on us alone — through help, an encounter, support from outside. From her point of view, one could also say that addiction is often connected with being uprooted: a person lacks roots, bonds, a place among people. So the way out is not only an inner struggle but also rebuilding connections with others.
addiction.practice: Think: is there a person or a group you could talk to about this without being judged? Simply note this possibility, without deciding anything.

hangover.text: The morning after is hard: the body aches, and inside there is anxiety, shame, gaps in memory. Simone Weil wrote about how imagination hurries to fill a void. From her point of view, one could say that the gaps in last night are especially easily filled with the darkest pictures: “I must have said something terrible.” Instead of imagination, Weil proposed attention to reality: to what is actually known. You don't need to justify yourself or punish yourself. You can take care of the body that is suffering now, and let the gap in memory stay empty for the time being. Later, more calmly, you can find out what really happened — and then respond to reality rather than to fear.
hangover.practice: Divide a page into two halves: “what I know for sure” and “what fear is filling in.” Fill in both — and notice the difference.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is bright and alive, and there's no need to spoil it. Simone Weil wrote about beauty as something we desire without trying to possess it: we want to look at what is beautiful, not to “eat” it. From her point of view, one could say that euphoria can be lived the same way — by contemplating it, not by trying to hold on to it by force. Trying to prolong the high at any cost is already “gravity,” reaching for compensation. Living it attentively, however, lets you take in this light without clinging to it. Euphoria is a moment when the world seems especially open. You can simply live it in all its fullness and notice what exactly is making you so glad right now.
euphoria.practice: Pause and name three things that seem especially vivid right now. Just look at them, without trying to prolong the moment.

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high can be painful: a moment ago everything was shining, and now it's heavy. Simone Weil described “gravity” as a natural law of the soul: whatever has risen tends to come down, just as objects fall. This is not a punishment and not proof that the high was a deception. It's simply how human nature works. From her point of view, one could say that the crash is not a failure but a manifestation of gravity, which shouldn't be taken as the truth about yourself or the world. Weil did not propose fighting it with effort; she spoke of patience, and of how what helps us rise is what comes of its own accord. You can give yourself time, without drawing conclusions at the lowest point.
crash.practice: Tell yourself: “This is gravity after a high; it will pass.” Do one small thing that looks after you — a cup of tea, some fresh air.

panic.text: A panic attack is very frightening: your heart pounds, you can't get enough air, it seems something irreparable is about to happen. In a moment like this there's no need to think about philosophy. But Simone Weil has a thought that can help in a simple way: attention directed at something concrete and real brings us back into the world. She taught looking at things clearly and slowly. A wave of panic usually builds, peaks and subsides within a few minutes. You can let it pass, holding on with your attention to what is near — the solid floor, an object in your hand, a sound. The heaviness of an object, its weight, its realness — all of this is support while the wave passes.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and feel their weight. Make your exhale longer than your inhale. Name five objects you can see — slowly, one at a time.

dread.text: Existential dread — “what is all this for?”, the sense of an abyss — can overwhelm you completely. Simone Weil looked at the world without illusions: she saw “necessity” in it — impersonal laws that don't ask what we want. But she also wrote that this necessity can be beautiful. Her example: the sea is no less beautiful to us because ships sometimes sink in it — the beauty of the world and its indifference to us cannot be separated. From this point of view, one could say that dread before the vastness of the world and wonder at it are two faces of one experience. You don't need to decide right now what the meaning of everything is. You can simply look at the sky, at a tree, and let yourself be part of this great world.
dread.practice: Go outside or step up to a window. Look at the sky or at a tree for a whole minute, demanding nothing of yourself.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives while you're not where you should be is very familiar. Simone Weil set imagination against reality: imagination paints bright pictures full of life that turn out, in fact, to be mere fantasy. From her point of view, one could say that the fear of missing out is a gaze fixed on the imagined lives of others. Weil stressed that real life means taking part in what is real: in a particular place, with particular people, in a particular task. She called this rootedness. A life seen in a feed has no roots. Your own life, even if it isn't so bright right now, is real. Bringing your attention back to it is not a consolation but a return to what actually is.
fomo.practice: Put your phone aside and name three things that are real in your life right now — a place, a person, a task.

sleepless.text: Insomnia and 3 a.m. thoughts are a hard combination. At night, when nothing distracts you, imagination becomes especially loud. Simone Weil wrote that imagination hurries to fill any void — and the silence of the night looks to it like a void that needs to be occupied. From her point of view, one could say that nighttime thoughts are not always the truth about your life but rather imagination at work in the dark. Instead, Weil proposed patient attention and waiting. You don't need to solve what is spinning in your head right now. You can simply lie in the quiet, without demanding that you fall asleep, and let the night be. Sometimes that is enough for the body to remember again how to rest.
sleepless.practice: Place your palm on your chest and slowly feel it rise and fall. Don't try to fall asleep — just follow your breathing.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply, and this pain is completely legitimate. Simone Weil wrote about how painful it is to discover that we loved not the real person but an image created by our imagination. This doesn't mean you are to blame: trust is not a mistake but a way of loving. But the gap between the image and the reality can be agonizing. From Weil's point of view, one could say that betrayal is a painful encounter with the reality of another person, which turned out to be different from what you hoped. Weil did not demand that we quickly forgive or understand. She proposed looking at reality clearly, without turning away — and this, though painful, can gradually become something to stand on.
betrayal.practice: Write down: what exactly was destroyed — your image of the person, trust, shared plans? Name it concretely, without judging yourself.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonizing: the fear of losing, the wish to hold on. Simone Weil wrote about love as consent to distance: to truly love means accepting that the other person is separate, free, and does not belong to us. She believed that the desire to possess another is a manifestation of “gravity,” not love in its pure form. From her point of view, one could say that jealousy is love mixed with the fear of loss. There's no need to be ashamed of it. But you can notice that in jealousy, attention is often turned toward imagined scenarios rather than toward the real person. Weil proposed returning to reality: what do you actually know, and what is fear filling in?
jealousy.practice: Write down one jealous thought, and next to it, what you know for sure. Notice the difference between imagination and reality.

resentment.text: Long-held resentment is a heavy burden, and it didn't appear out of nowhere: you really were hurt. Simone Weil wrote about “the forgiveness of debts.” She meant that we often expect the past to give back what it owes us — an apology, justice, lost time. Weil considered this expectation very human, but also very heavy. From her point of view, one could say that resentment is a bill we keep presenting. For Weil, forgiving a debt is neither an obligation nor an excuse for the one who hurt you, but an acceptance that the past will not pay back what it took. This can free up room for the present. But there's no need to hurry: it happens when you are ready.
resentment.practice: Write down what you are “owed” in this situation. Don't try to cancel the debt — just look at it directly.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart is one of the sharpest pains, and it deserves time and gentleness. Simone Weil wrote about love as attention to the reality of another person. When a relationship ends, we lose not only the person but also the future we imagined together. Weil said that imagination hurries to fill the void: with fantasies of how things could have been, with reproaches, with dreams of getting back together. From her point of view, one could say that these fantasies are understandable, but they prolong the pain. You don't need to forbid yourself to grieve. But you can little by little bring your attention back to reality: to yourself, to your days, to what you received from this love. The void a person leaves behind can, in time, become a place for something new.
heartbreak.practice: Write down one thing you learned about yourself in this relationship that you want to keep.

impostor.text: The feeling that you're about to be found out is familiar to a great many people. In her essay on school studies, Simone Weil wrote that the value of an effort of attention doesn't depend on the result: even if the problem isn't solved, the attention put into it is not lost. She advised looking at your mistakes calmly and attentively, without self-abasement — as part of learning. From her point of view, one could say that impostor syndrome measures you against an imagined ideal. Weil proposed looking at reality instead: at what you actually do and what you are learning. Real effort, even imperfect, is not a fake. It is exactly what mastery grows from.
impostor.practice: Write down one mistake you made recently and one thing it taught you. Look at it as a teacher, not as a judge.

self_hatred.text: Self-hatred is a very heavy feeling, and you don't have to agree with its verdict. Simone Weil described precisely how severe pain and humiliation leave a brand of self-contempt on the soul, as though the person were to blame for their own suffering. She saw in this the trace of a wound, not the truth about the person. Weil has the concept of “decreation,” which is sometimes misunderstood. Decreation is neither destruction nor self-hatred: Weil herself distinguished it from destruction. It is loosening the ego's grip to make room for attention to the world and to others. From this point of view, self-hatred is the opposite — an agonizing fixation on one's own image. You are allowed to treat yourself with the same gentleness you would show another person who is suffering.
self_hatred.practice: Imagine someone close to you saying these words about themselves. What would you answer them? Say it to yourself.

helplessness.text: Being powerless to change anything is one of the hardest experiences. Simone Weil knew it well: she saw how factory workers were turned into appendages of machines, how war stripped people of all power over their fate. In her essay on the Iliad she showed how force turns a person into a thing. Weil did not say that helplessness is your fault. She saw it as a consequence of how the world and society are arranged. But she also stressed that even in helplessness the possibility of attention remains: to see clearly what is happening and not to turn away from others who suffer nearby. From her point of view, one could say that attention is something that can't be taken away completely. It isn't omnipotence, but it isn't nothing either.
helplessness.practice: Name one thing you can direct your attention to right now — a person, a task, a detail around you. Stay with it for a minute.

procrastination.text: When you can't get started, it's easy to blame yourself for laziness, but things are usually more complicated. In her essay on school studies, Simone Weil wrote that attention is not muscular strain. We often think we need to pull ourselves together, grit our teeth, and then it will work. But such strain, for Weil, tends to get in the way. Real attention is openness, almost a kind of waiting. From her point of view, one could say that procrastination is sometimes born of fear of the huge effort that seems necessary. Weil, however, advised treating work as an exercise: what matters is not the result but the attentive effort itself, even a small one. That way you can begin without demanding a lot of yourself all at once.
procrastination.practice: Choose the smallest piece of the task and give it five minutes of calm attention — without aiming to finish.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home is a deep pain, and Simone Weil devoted an entire book to it. She wrote The Need for Roots in London in 1943, a refugee herself, cut off from her native France. For Weil, rootedness is participation in the life of a community that preserves treasures of the past and expectations of the future: through place, language, work, people. She called the loss of roots one of the most dangerous diseases that can strike a person and a society. From this point of view, your pain is not a weakness but a response to the loss of one of the soul's deepest needs. Roots, for Weil, can also be put down anew: by taking part in the life of a new place, through habits, connections, work, language.
uprooted.practice: Name one small “rooting” thing you could do in the new place: a ritual, a place you go to, a person you talk with.

quote.text: To be rooted is perhaps the most important and least recognized need of the human soul.
quote.author: Simone Weil

overload.text: Overload and the endless feed wear you out — attention splinters, and you can't concentrate on anything. For Simone Weil, attention was the most precious thing a person has. She wrote of it as the rarest form of generosity and almost as prayer. Working in a factory, she saw how the speed and monotony of labor destroy the ability to think. From her point of view, one could say that informational noise works in a similar way: attention torn into a thousand little pieces stops being attention. This is not your fault; these are the conditions we live in. But attention can gradually be gathered again: by directing it at one thing at a time, slowly and wholly.
overload.practice: Choose one thing — tea, a window, a page of a book — and give it all your attention for two minutes, with no phone nearby.

unreality.text: The feeling that everything is somehow not real can be frightening, and it deserves respectful attention. For Simone Weil, “reality” was a key word. She believed that contact with reality happens above all through the body and through work: through the weight of an object, the resistance of material, the effort of muscles. It's no accident her book is called Gravity and Grace: for her, gravity is also the weight of the world, its realness. From this point of view, one could say that when the sense of reality is muted, what helps you return is not reflection but simple physical contact with the world. Things go on having weight and shape, even when everything inside feels far away.
unreality.practice: Pick up something heavy — a book, a cup of water. Feel its weight, temperature, texture. Slowly describe them to yourself.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a precious feeling. For Simone Weil, the beauty of the world was one of the most direct paths to what is greater than us. She wrote that beauty is something we desire without trying to possess it: we want to look at what is beautiful, not own it. In awe this is especially clear: we don't want to take anything, we simply look. Weil saw in the beauty of the world an order and a necessity in which one can sense the harmony of the whole. From this point of view, one could say that awe is pure attention that demands nothing. It is worth simply living it: letting yourself be small before something great — and there will be no humiliation in this, only joy.
awe.practice: Stay for one more minute with whatever filled you with awe. Don't photograph or describe it — just look.

relief.text: Relief is like an exhale after long tension. You can simply live it. Simone Weil contrasted “gravity” and “grace”: gravity pulls downward, while grace comes on its own, not as the result of our efforts. From her point of view, one could say that relief sometimes resembles grace: it comes unexpectedly, when the load suddenly grows lighter. There's no need to immediately look for explanations or think about the next problem. Weil valued the ability to receive gifts without appropriating them. Relief is such a gift. You can pause and notice: what has changed in your body, your breathing, your gaze? This too is part of reality, and it deserves attention no less than the hard moments do.
relief.practice: Take a slow exhale and notice where in your body you feel the relief. Stay with it for a few breaths.

calm.text: Calm is a valuable state, and it needs no justification. For Simone Weil, calm was connected with attention and waiting: the ability to be open without demanding anything. She wrote that attention, taken to its highest degree, becomes like prayer — for her, a believer, this was meant literally, but a non-religious reader can also sense what she means: a full, quiet openness to what is. From this point of view, one could say that calm is not the absence of life but a particular fullness of it. Weil also spoke of consent to necessity — to the way the world is. Calm can be that kind of consent: the world is as it is, and right now that is enough.
calm.practice: Spend a minute in silence, doing nothing. Notice three things that simply are right now — a sound, the light, your breath.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is the moment when new ideas and images arrive. Simone Weil wrote that we receive the most precious gifts not when we chase them but when we know how to wait for them. Attention, for her, is not strained effort but an open readiness to receive whatever comes. From this point of view, inspiration resembles grace: it comes by itself, but it comes to where there is room for it. Weil believed that this room is made by attention — patient, lengthy, sometimes seemingly fruitless. So inspiration is not an accident but a response to the openness you may have long been cultivating in yourself. It's worth catching while it's fresh.
inspiration.practice: Write down the idea right now, as it is, without correcting it. Then thank yourself for being ready to receive it.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is a shameful feeling, but Simone Weil probably wouldn't judge you for it: she carefully studied such “low” movements of the soul. In Gravity and Grace she described a law resembling a physical one: a suffering person tries somehow to lessen their suffering — for instance, by passing it outward or by feeling that they are not the only one down below. She attributed all this to “gravity” — a natural movement of the soul that happens on its own, without our choosing. From her point of view, one could say that schadenfreude often reveals not malice but one's own accumulated pain: someone else's failure balances the scales for a moment. Weil did not propose fighting gravity by force. She proposed attention: seeing what is happening inside without turning away — and then the feeling itself already begins to change.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself quietly: “What pain of my own felt lighter for a moment because of someone else's failure?” Just name it.

contempt.text: Contempt arises easily — toward those who seem stupid, weak or unworthy. Simone Weil thought a great deal about how people stop seeing one another as human. In her essay “The Iliad, or the Poem of Force” she shows that force turns a person into a thing — both the one who endures it and the one who wields it. From her point of view, one could say that contempt is also a small form of such force: in our gaze, another person turns from someone alive into “a nobody.” The opposite of this, for Weil, is attention: the ability to see the real person, not an image created by our irritation. This doesn't require agreeing with them or approving of what they do. But attention restores fullness to both you and them — and often shows that behind the contempt there was tiredness or hurt.
contempt.practice: Think of a person you feel contempt for and silently name one real, concrete detail of their life that has nothing to do with your judgment of them.

disgust.text: Disgust — toward people, a situation, sometimes yourself — is a strong bodily feeling, and it isn't chosen. Simone Weil knew a world that few philosophers have seen from the inside: she worked in a factory, amid noise, dirt and an exhausting pace, and wrote about it in her Factory Journal without squeamishness and without prettifying anything. Her central idea is attention: looking at reality as it is, without replacing it with what imagination paints. From her point of view, one could say that disgust often concerns not the thing itself but the image we have built around it. Weil did not demand suppressing this feeling. She suggested letting your gaze linger a little longer than you want to — and then, in what repels you, something simply human, fragile, in need, sometimes shows through.
disgust.practice: Describe what disgusts you in three neutral words, as an observer would. Notice whether the strength of the feeling has changed.

revenge.text: The desire for revenge is a natural response to harm done, and Simone Weil understood how it works. In Gravity and Grace she described how a person who has been hurt tends to pass the pain on, as though that would restore a broken balance. She attributed this to “gravity”: a movement of the soul that happens almost by itself, like an object falling. But Weil believed it is possible not to be a mere transmitter of evil. Her image is of a person in whom evil stops instead of continuing. This does not mean staying silent about what happened or agreeing with it: Weil fought injustice all her life. It means giving up only one thing — the wish for the other person to suffer in the same way. From her point of view, noticing a thirst for revenge in yourself is nothing to be ashamed of: it is the first step toward keeping it from ruling you.
revenge.practice: Write down what was done to you. Then write what you actually need now: recognition, protection, justice, peace? Choose one thing that can be achieved without harm.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at loved ones — a partner, parents, children — is inevitable, because they are the people we live closest to. Simone Weil wrote that the soul constantly creates images of other people in the imagination, and we love and wait for these images more than for the people themselves. A person close to us inevitably doesn't match our picture, and irritation is born of that mismatch. From her point of view, one could say that anger at loved ones is often anger at the gap between the imagined and the real. Weil called attention to the real person one of the hardest forms of love. This doesn't mean the anger is wrong: sometimes it points to a real injustice. But the shame after an outburst doesn't have to become a punishment. It's better to ask: whom did I just see — a living person, or my picture of them?
anger_at_loved.practice: Write: “I expected them to…” and “But right now they actually…” Just look at the difference.

ambivalence.text: To love a person and at the same time be unable to stand them is a hard but honest state. Simone Weil valued contradictions and believed there's no need to hurry to resolve them. In Gravity and Grace she wrote that when the mind runs up against a contradiction that cannot be removed, it can become something like a lever — a way of seeing reality more deeply. From her point of view, one could say that mixed feelings toward someone close are neither a mistake nor a sign of poor love. They are a sign that you see the person whole, not as a convenient image. Imagination wants to simplify everything: either they are good or they are bad. Attention allows you to hold both feelings at once, crossing out neither. A love that contains both tenderness and irritation is not lesser but truer.
ambivalence.practice: Write on one line: “What I love in you is… and what I find hard is your…” Keep both parts, without choosing between them.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, a departure, or even the death of a loved one who was ill for a long time is often hidden even from ourselves. Simone Weil wrote about “affliction” — a particular mixture of suffering, powerlessness and loneliness that weighs not only on the one who is suffering but also on those nearby. Caring for such a person, or living alongside long-lasting pain, means carrying a very heavy load for years. From her point of view, one could say that relief is the natural response of a soul from which a weight has been lifted. It does not mean you loved less. Weil distinguished reality from imagination: imagination paints a picture in which the “right” kind of person should feel only grief. Reality is more complicated: love and relief can exist in you at the same time, and neither cancels the other.
guilty_relief.practice: Let yourself say aloud or write: “I feel lighter. And I loved.” Sit for a minute with these words, adding nothing.

indifference.text: Sometimes where something “should” move you, there is emptiness — and on top of that emptiness comes worry about yourself. Simone Weil wrote about “affliction” and showed that intense suffering can cause numbness: the soul seems to stop feeling in order to endure. She also spoke of the void as a state that doesn't need to be filled in a hurry — where there is room, something new may come. From her point of view, one could say that indifference doesn't necessarily mean callousness. Sometimes it's tiredness, sometimes protection, sometimes simply a pause. Weil valued honesty before reality more than a display of the right feelings. If right now you don't feel what you're “supposed” to, you can admit it without shame. Attention, for Weil, doesn't require emotions — you can look at a person or an event honestly, without strong feelings.
indifference.practice: Look for one minute at what “should” move you — attentively, but without demanding any feelings of yourself. Just look.

escape.text: Simone Weil would probably have understood from the inside the wish to drop everything — a job, a city, a role. She herself left teaching to work in a factory for a year, and later changed places and occupations more than once. In The Need for Roots she described the needs of the soul, and among them are not only order and rootedness but also the need for risk, for liberty, for responsibility. When life becomes monotonous and devoid of meaning, the soul, for Weil, suffers from it the way a body suffers from hunger. From her point of view, one could say that the desire to escape is a signal of an unmet need, not a whim. But Weil also warned of “compensations” — imaginary worlds the soul flees to from reality. It's worth asking attentively: what exactly am I missing — and is there room for it here?
escape.practice: Complete the sentence: “What I'm missing is…” (risk? freedom? meaning? respect?). Choose one word and notice where in your life it is completely absent.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone unavailable or “wrong” can be strong and confusing. Simone Weil wrote a great deal about desire and did not consider it trivial: in it she saw the soul's pull toward goodness and beauty, even if aimed somewhere other than we expect. She noticed that beauty awakens in us the desire to possess, to take hold, and she saw in this a deep human drama. From her point of view, one could say that attraction shows what fullness, beauty or aliveness your soul is reaching for. Weil gave no ready-made answers about what to do with desire. She suggested first looking — attentively and honestly, without filling in the picture with imagination. Sometimes behind an attraction to a particular person lies a thirst for a quality of life you are missing.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Ask yourself, without naming the person: “What quality of life do I feel alongside this attraction — aliveness, tenderness, freedom, risk?”

quote.text: The great trouble in human life is that looking and eating are two different operations.
quote.author: Simone Weil
quote.source: “Forms of the Implicit Love of God,” in Waiting for God

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment can freeze you and drain your strength. Simone Weil knew it: she was shy and awkward, and often felt like an outsider both in academic circles and in the factory. Her notion of attention helps with this fear in an unexpected way. Attention, for Weil, is turned away from oneself — toward reality, toward another person. Social anxiety, by contrast, turns the gaze inward: how do I look, what will they think of me. From her point of view, one could say that relief comes not from being liked but from forgetting yourself a little by becoming genuinely interested in the other person. Weil wrote that the ability to ask another what they are going through is a rare gift. Try shifting your attention to the person beside you — not to come across better, but simply out of curiosity about them.
social_anxiety.practice: In your next conversation, ask one sincere question about the other person and listen attentively to the whole answer. Notice what happens to your anxiety meanwhile.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is hard: the mind wants to fill the void with an answer, even a frightening one. Simone Weil saw this movement of the soul. She wrote that imagination strives to “fill the void” — and then we invent scenarios that seem more real than reality itself. Weil proposed another path — attention: the ability not to grab the first thought, to stay open and wait until reality reveals itself. She described attention in her essay on school studies: it is not muscular tension or an effort of will but rather a calm readiness. From her point of view, one could say that uncertainty is a space that doesn't have to be filled with anxious pictures. You can admit, “I don't know” — and stay in that not-knowing a little longer, without turning away from it.
uncertainty.practice: When your mind starts painting scenarios, tell yourself: “This is imagination.” Then name three things you can see right now.

quote.text: Attention consists of suspending our thought, leaving it detached, empty, and ready to be penetrated by the object.
quote.author: Simone Weil
quote.source: “Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies” (1942)

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, results, news — can be agonizing. But for Simone Weil, waiting was not an empty waste of time but one of the soul's central states. Her posthumous collection is called Waiting for God, and in her essay on school studies she wrote that what is most valuable cannot be seized by effort — it can only be waited for, attentively. Weil distinguished tense, impatient waiting, which wears you out, from patient, open waiting, in which a person doesn't cling to a particular outcome. From her point of view, one could say that waiting is agonizing as long as imagination paints answers in place of reality. But it can be lived differently — as a pause in which you are attentive to what is here now. This won't cancel the anxiety, but it will make the waiting a little less empty.
waiting.practice: When you feel the urge to check whether the answer has come, take three slow breaths and notice one thing in the present moment. Only then check.

quote.text: We do not obtain the most precious gifts by going in search of them but by waiting for them.
quote.author: Simone Weil
quote.source: “Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies” (1942)

regret.text: Regret over something done or left undone can hold on for a long time. Simone Weil had deep respect for reality, including the past: what has happened is already part of the world and can't be rewritten. But she distinguished two attitudes toward mistakes. One is tormenting self-accusation, which in essence still revolves around the “I.” The other is attention: a calm, honest look at what happened, with no attempt either to justify or to punish yourself. In her essay on school studies she advised students to examine their mistakes attentively, without turning away from them — that is how one learns. From her point of view, one could say that regret is valuable when it becomes knowledge rather than punishment. The past can't be changed, but you can understand what it teaches — and that knowledge already changes the present.
regret.practice: Describe the mistake as you would describe it for a student: what happened, what was unclear then, what is clear now. Without judging yourself.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is a pain in which love is especially visible. Simone Weil wrote about love for someone absent, about how hard it is to bear the void left in the other's place. The soul strives to fill it: with imagined conversations, fantasies of meeting, reproaches. Weil called such fillers “compensations” and did not condemn them, but suggested sometimes leaving the place empty — not out of asceticism, but out of respect for reality. The absent person is real even when they aren't near, and your love for them is real too. From her point of view, one could say that longing is love that for now cannot show itself in presence. It can be lived not as a lack but as a special form of faithfulness to someone dear to you.
longing.practice: Recall one real, concrete detail of this person — a gesture, an intonation. Stay with it for a minute without turning it into a fantasy.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — wars, injustice, the suffering of people you will never meet — can be enormous. Simone Weil felt it all her life: as a child she gave up sugar on learning that the soldiers at the front had none, and later she worked in a factory to share the lives of workers. Her main answer to others' suffering is attention. She believed that true love of one's neighbor begins by simply seeing a person in trouble and asking what they are going through. From her point of view, one could say: you cannot hold all the pain of the world, but you can truly see at least one person who is struggling. This small form of attention is not an escape from the great pain but an honest, doable response to it.
world_pain.practice: Choose one real person who is struggling right now — nearby or far away. Ask them today how they are, and listen without giving advice.

quote.text: The love of our neighbor in all its fullness simply means being able to say to him: “What are you going through?”
quote.author: Simone Weil
quote.source: “Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies” (1942)

rejection.text: Rejection hurts: as if you went unnoticed or were deemed unnecessary. Simone Weil knew this: she was not always taken seriously — not in academic circles, not in political movements, not among the workers, to whom she seemed strange. Her ideas about attention are connected with how hard it is to truly see another person. Most people, Weil wrote, look at others through imagination — they see their own expectations, not the real person. From her point of view, one could say that rejection often speaks of what the other person failed or didn't have time to see, not of your worth. That doesn't make it less painful. But you can acknowledge the pain without agreeing with the conclusion that you are worthless. The reality of you is larger than someone else's passing glance.
rejection.practice: Write down: “I wasn't seen when…” And next to it: “There is something in me worth seeing: …” — name one thing honestly.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned is one of the most ancient fears. Simone Weil wrote about “roots”: a person needs to be part of a community that preserves something of the past and expects something of the future. In The Need for Roots she called rootedness perhaps the most important and least recognized need of the soul. From her point of view, one could say that the fear of abandonment is the fear of losing roots, connection, support. It speaks not of your weakness but of a deep human need. Weil did not propose getting rid of this need. She said that roots grow from many connections: people, place, work, language, a shared cause, tradition. When there are roots in different places, the loss of one connection doesn't bring everything down. The fear can be softened by tending to your roots rather than clinging to one person.
abandonment.practice: Draw a small tree and label its roots: the people, places and activities that hold you. Mark one root that deserves your attention.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love wounds painfully, because love longs for meeting. Simone Weil wrote about love in a very unexpected way: she believed that pure love includes consent to the distance between yourself and the one you love. For her this is not a renunciation of feeling but a recognition of the other's freedom and reality. The beloved is not an extension of our desires but a separate world. From her point of view, one could say that unrequited love is painful precisely because the distance is imposed, not chosen. Weil did not propose forcing yourself to “let go.” But she showed that even without an answer, your love could have been genuine — attention to a real person. That capacity stays with you, and the fact that it went unanswered doesn't cancel it.
unrequited.practice: Write down three things you saw in this person that were truly theirs, not your fantasy. Let them simply be.

quote.text: To love purely is to consent to distance, it is to adore the distance between ourselves and that which we love.
quote.author: Simone Weil

humiliation.text: Humiliation wounds more deeply than many other feelings. Simone Weil knew it from the inside: in the factory she experienced firsthand how foremen treated workers, and wrote that her very sense of her own dignity was almost erased there. In The Need for Roots she named honor as one of the basic needs of the soul, and she included social humiliation in her notion of “affliction” — alongside pain and loneliness. Weil stressed that humiliation speaks of the force that was applied to a person, not of their worth. Force, in the words of her essay on the Iliad, turns a person into a thing — but it is the force that does this, not the person. From her point of view, you can acknowledge the full weight of humiliation — and refuse to believe what it tries to tell you about yourself.
humiliation.practice: Write: “I was treated like…, but I am…” Finish the second part in a way that is true about you.

quote.text: Those who are unhappy have no need for anything in this world but people capable of giving them their attention.
quote.author: Simone Weil
quote.source: “Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies” (1942)

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is often born of comparison with images. Simone Weil distinguished reality from imagination: imagination, she said, constantly paints pictures that seem brighter and more “correct” than what is real. We look at the body not with our own eyes but with the eyes of an imagined judge, and compare it with images that don't exist in reality. For Weil, the body was first of all something that works, gets tired, feels, touches the world. She wrote about the beauty of the world as an order that includes our bodies too, with all their particularities. From her point of view, one could say that attention to the real body — not to a picture, but to what it does and feels — weakens the power of the imagined model. The body doesn't have to match an image to be part of the world.
body_shame.practice: Choose a part of your body you criticize and name one thing it does for you every day.

illness.text: Illness — when the body lets you down — changes everything: plans, strength, your very sense of yourself. For many years Simone Weil lived with severe, exhausting headaches that kept her from working and thinking. She wrote about “affliction” — a state in which physical pain joins with loneliness and the feeling that no one is interested in you anymore. Weil stressed that such suffering is hard to see from the outside: people look away. That is why attention is so valuable — both from others and your own toward yourself. From her point of view, one could say that illness doesn't make you less, even when it takes away your strength. Weil did not romanticize suffering or look for justifications in it. She proposed not turning away: acknowledging the weight, and giving yourself and others the chance to be near it.
illness.practice: Name one person you can honestly tell how you are feeling. If you like, write them a few words today.

pride.text: Pride in what you've done is a healthy feeling, and a deserved one. Simone Weil was wary of the “I,” yet she highly valued the joy of work well done. Working in the factory, she saw how workers were deprived of this joy: they never saw the result of their labor and didn't understand what their part was for. In The Need for Roots she wrote that a person needs to see the meaning of their work and to feel satisfaction in it — this is part of dignity. From her point of view, one could say that healthy pride is not superiority over others but joy in touching reality through your own effort and attention. You made something, and the world is a little different because of you. You can quietly and honestly be glad of this — without apologizing and without comparing.
pride.practice: Look at what you've done for one minute — attentively, as if it were someone else's work. Name one detail that turned out well.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness is a quiet state in which sorrow mingles with something tender and clear. Simone Weil wrote about the beauty of the world and about how beauty is always a little sad: it can't be possessed, held on to or eaten — it can only be looked at. It is this distance, for Weil, that makes beauty pure. From her point of view, one could say that melancholy is a feeling in which we experience the impossibility of possessing what we love: a sunset, the past, a moment. It is neither an illness nor a weakness but a special sensitivity to the fragility of the world. Weil did not urge getting rid of this feeling. She saw in it a seed of attention: the ability to look without demanding anything. Gentle sadness can simply be lived — as quiet contemplation of what is passing.
melancholy.practice: Find one beautiful thing near you and look at it for a minute, wanting nothing from it — neither to keep it nor to photograph it.
